title: Nessus. Herculis mors
titleEn: The Crossing and the Bloodied Robe — Metamorphoses IX.98–171
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: The Euenus is in flood, and Hercules trusts his new wife Deianira to the centaur Nessus to be carried across while he swims himself; Nessus tries to make off with her, takes an arrow steeped in the Hydra’s poison in the back, and dying gives her his blood-soaked garment, presenting it as a charm to bring love back. Long afterwards, hearing that Hercules is held by a passion for Iole, she sends him that garment, and the sacrifice he is making to Jove at Cenaeum becomes the beginning of his death.

advisory.lede: In these lines the centaur Nessus, entrusted with carrying Hercules’ wife Deianira across a flooded river, tries to carry her off and rape her.
advisory.more: The poem is direct about it. Nessus is a trustee absconding with what was left in his keeping; Hercules names the act a forbidden coupling and throws his father Ixion’s punishment for the same crime in his face; and afterwards Ovid calls Deianira simply “the woman he had seized”. Nessus is shot before he gets clear, but the attempt is the hinge of the whole part — his revenge for it is what kills Hercules. Lectorium renders all of this at the force the Latin carries, in both English layers, and the text is presented unaltered.

sentences.t:
Hunc tamen ablati domuit iactura decoris,
cetera sospes habet;
sentences.l: Him, however, the loss of his carried-off glory subdued; the rest he keeps, himself unhurt;
sentences.i: Still, the loss of that torn-away glory broke him; safe otherwise, he keeps the rest;
sentences.n: “sospes” is nominative and describes him, not “cetera”: apart from the one loss he is unhurt, and “ablati … decoris”, “of the glory carried off”, packs a whole clause into a participle. Magnus prints “Hunc … domuit”, “the loss subdued him”; some editions print “Huic … doluit”, “the loss was a grief to him”.

sentences.t:
capitis quoque fronde saligna
aut super inposita celatur harundine damnum.
sentences.l: the damage to his head, too, is concealed with willow-leaf or with reed laid over it.
sentences.i: The damage to his head, too, is kept out of sight under willow-leaf, or under a reed laid across.
sentences.n: “quoque” here is the ordinary adverb, “too”, not the “quo-que” (“and with which”) that ambushes readers elsewhere; “fronde saligna” and “inposita harundine” are ablatives of means. The dressing is the river-god’s own vegetation: willow and reed grow on his banks — the “decus” he has lost from his head is a horn.

sentences.t:
At te, Nesse ferox, eiusdem virginis ardor
perdiderat volucri traiectum terga sagitta.
sentences.l: But you, fierce Nessus, passion for the same girl had destroyed, pierced through the back by a flying arrow.
sentences.i: But you, savage Nessus, passion for that same girl had already destroyed, shot through the back by an arrow in flight.
sentences.n: Ovid turns aside to address a character directly — apostrophe, which he uses again on Deianira at line 138. “traiectum terga” is a Greek accusative of respect after a passive participle, “pierced as to the back”, with the poetic plural “terga” for one back, and the pluperfect “perdiderat” gives the ending away before the story starts.

sentences.t:
Namque nova repetens patrios cum coniuge muros
venerat Eueni rapidas Iove natus ad undas.
sentences.l: For, seeking again his ancestral walls with his new wife, the one born of Jove had come to the swift waters of the Euenus.
sentences.i: For the son of Jove, on his way back to his ancestral walls with his new bride, had come to the rushing water of the Euenus.
sentences.n: “Iove natus”, “born from Jove”, is a periphrasis for Hercules with an ablative of origin, and “nova … cum coniuge” splits around its preposition in the ordinary poetic way. The Euenus is the river of Aetolia, the country of the bride he is bringing home.

sentences.t:
Uberior solito, nimbis hiemalibus auctus
verticibusque frequens erat atque inpervius amnis.
sentences.l: Fuller than usual, swollen by winter storm-clouds and crowded with whirlpools, the river was, and not to be crossed.
sentences.i: The river ran fuller than its wont, swollen with winter rain, thick with eddies and impassable.
sentences.n: “solito” is an ablative of comparison after the comparative “uberior”: fuller than is customary. “frequens” with an ablative means “thick with, crowded with” — the whirlpools are what it is full of — and the subject “amnis” is withheld to the very last word.

sentences.t:
Intrepidum pro se, curam de coniuge agentem
Nessus adit, membrisque valens scitusque vadorum,
sentences.l: Him, undaunted on his own account, but carrying anxiety about his wife, Nessus approaches — strong in his limbs and knowing the fords —
sentences.i: Nessus comes up to him, fearless for himself but taken up with worry for his wife; and Nessus is strong of limb and knows the crossings.
sentences.n: The accusative participial phrases “intrepidum … agentem” have no noun of their own: Hercules is supplied from the sense, and “curam agere de” is “to be concerned about”. “membris valens” (ablative of respect) and “scitus vadorum” (genitive after “scitus”) give the centaur’s two qualifications, and both are the pretext for the offer he is about to make.

sentences.t:
“officio” que “meo ripa sistetur in illa
haec,” ait “Alcide. Tu viribus utere nando!”
sentences.l: “By my service,” he says, “this woman here will be set down on that bank yonder, Alcides. You, make use of your strength by swimming!”
sentences.i: “My service will land her on the far bank there, Alcides,” he says. “Put your own strength into the swim.”
sentences.n: The enclitic “-que” is printed outside the quotation marks because it joins the sentence and not the speech: read “officioque meo”. “sistetur” is future passive; “haec”, “this woman here”, is set against “in illa ripa”, “on that bank over there”; “utere” is the imperative of the deponent “utor” with its ablative “viribus”, and “nando” is an ablative gerund, “by swimming”.

sentences.t:
pallentemque metu fluviumque ipsumque timentem
tradidit Aonius pavidam Calydonida Nesso.
sentences.l: and her, pale with fear and fearing both the river and the man himself, the Aonian handed over — the frightened woman of Calydon — to Nessus.
sentences.i: And so the Aonian handed the Calydonian girl to Nessus: pale with fear, afraid of the river and of Nessus himself, and trembling.
sentences.n: Four accusatives agree together — “pallentem”, “timentem”, “pavidam”, “Calydonida”, the Greek accusative of “Calydonis”, the woman of Calydon, Deianira. “ipsum” is Nessus: she is afraid of the ferryman as well as of the water, and the line says so one word before she is handed to him; “Aonius”, “the Aonian”, is Hercules by his Boeotian birth.

sentences.t:
Mox, ut erat, pharetraque gravis spolioque leonis
(nam clavam et curvos trans ripam miserat arcus),
“quandoquidem coepi, superentur flumina!” dixit,
sentences.l: Presently, just as he was, weighed down with quiver and the lion’s spoil (for he had thrown his club and his curved bow across to the far bank), he said: “Since I have begun, let the waters be beaten!”
sentences.i: Then, just as he stood, heavy with quiver and lionskin — he had already thrown club and curved bow to the other side — he said, “Since I have begun, let the river be beaten.”
sentences.n: “ut erat”, “as he was”, means he lays nothing down; “gravis” takes ablatives of respect, and the “spolium leonis” is the skin he wears. “superentur” is a jussive subjunctive in the passive, “let them be overcome” — his answer to a river in flood is to order it defeated, and “flumina” is a poetic plural for the one stream.

sentences.t:
nec dubitat nec, qua sit clementissimus amnis,
quaerit et obsequio deferri spernit aquarum.
sentences.l: and he does not hesitate, nor does he ask where the river is gentlest, and he scorns to be carried down by the compliance of the waters.
sentences.i: He does not hesitate; he does not look for the river’s kindest stretch; and he refuses to be swept downstream at the water’s convenience.
sentences.n: “qua sit clementissimus amnis” is an indirect question after “quaerit”, which is why “sit” is subjunctive. “obsequio aquarum deferri” is a passive infinitive after “spernit”: he will not let the current take him where it will, but means to cross straight.

sentences.t:
Iamque tenens ripam, missos cum tolleret arcus,
coniugis agnovit vocem:
sentences.l: And now, holding the bank, when he was lifting the bow he had thrown across, he recognized his wife’s voice:
sentences.i: And now, with the bank in his grip, as he was picking up the bow he had thrown over, he heard his wife’s voice and knew it:
sentences.n: “cum tolleret” is the circumstantial “cum” with the subjunctive, “at the moment when he was lifting”, and “missos … arcus” is the bow of line 114, the participle standing in for a relative clause. “agnovit” is not simply “heard”: he knew whose the cry was.

sentences.t:
Nessoque paranti
fallere depositum “quo te fiducia” clamat
“vana pedum, violente, rapit? Tibi, Nesse biformis,
dicimus. Exaudi nec res intercipe nostras!
sentences.l: and to Nessus, as he was preparing to cheat the trust, he shouts: “Where is the empty confidence of your feet carrying you off, you violent thing? To you, two-formed Nessus, we speak. Hear me out, and do not intercept what is mine!
sentences.i: and to Nessus, who was making ready to break the trust, he shouts: “Where is that empty confidence in your legs taking you, brute? You, two-shaped Nessus, are the one I am speaking to. Hear me, and keep your hands off what is mine.
sentences.n: “depositum” is the legal word for a thing handed over in trust to be given back, which is exactly what Deianira was at line 112: Nessus is not only a thief but a defaulting trustee. “fiducia … pedum” is an objective genitive, confidence placed in his feet; “dicimus” is the poetic plural for “I say”; “violente” is a vocative, and the contempt in it is Hercules’ own.

sentences.t:
Si te nulla mei reverentia movit, at orbes
concubitus vetitos poterant inhibere paterni.
sentences.l: If no respect for me has moved you, yet your father’s wheel could have checked forbidden couplings.
sentences.i: If no regard for me moved you, your father’s wheel might at least have held you back from a coupling that is forbidden.
sentences.n: “mei” is the objective genitive of “ego”, “respect for me”, not “my respect”. “orbes … paterni”, a poetic plural for one wheel, is the wheel Ixion turns on: Nessus’s father was destroyed for attempting Juno, that is, for precisely what Nessus is doing here, which is why the wheel “could have checked” it.

sentences.t:
Haud tamen effugies, quamvis ope fidis equina:
vulnere, non pedibus te consequar.”
sentences.l: Yet you will not get away, however much you trust in horse-strength: with a wound, not with feet, I shall overtake you.”
sentences.i: You will not get clear all the same, for all your trust in a horse’s power: I shall catch you with a wound, not with my feet.”
sentences.n: “fidis” is the second person of “fido”, which takes an ablative — “ope equina”, horse-power, the half of him that can outrun a man. The threat turns on two instrumental ablatives set against each other, “vulnere, non pedibus”: the running will be done by the arrow.

sentences.t:
Ultima dicta
res probat, et missa fugientia terga sagitta
traicit: exstabat ferrum de pectore aduncum.
sentences.l: The outcome proves the last words, and with an arrow shot he pierces the fleeing back: the barbed iron stood out from his chest.
sentences.i: The event made good his last words: the arrow he loosed went through the fleeing back, and the hooked iron stood out at the chest.
sentences.n: “missa … sagitta” is an ablative of instrument with a participle, “with an arrow shot”, not an ablative absolute: the subject of “traicit” is still Hercules, and “terga” is once more a poetic plural for one back. Magnus prints “res probat”, “the outcome proves his last words”; some editions print “re probat”, “he proves them by the deed”.

sentences.t:
Quod simul evulsum est, sanguis per utrumque foramen
emicuit mixtus Lernaei tabe veneni.
sentences.l: As soon as it had been torn out, blood spurted through each opening, mixed with the corruption of the Lernaean poison.
sentences.i: The moment it was wrenched out, blood leapt through both holes, mixed with the foul matter of the Lernaean venom.
sentences.n: “Quod” is a connecting relative picking up “ferrum”, “and when that was torn out”, and “simul” by itself here stands for “simul ac”, “as soon as”. Both holes, entry and exit, follow from the barb standing clear of the chest; the Lernaean poison is the Hydra’s, in which the arrows were dipped, and “tabes” is the ooze of a rotting thing.

sentences.t:
Excipit hunc Nessus “neque enim moriemur inulti”
secum ait
sentences.l: Nessus catches this, and says to himself, “for we shall not die unavenged,”
sentences.i: Nessus catches the blood as it comes. “I shall not die unavenged,” he says to himself,
sentences.n: “hunc” is the blood of the line before: the centaur has the presence of mind to collect the very thing that is killing him, and the present “excipit” pulls the moment up close. “moriemur inulti” is a future indicative used as a vow, with a poetic plural for “I”, and “neque enim” gives the reason for the catching: he means to have something to be avenged with.

sentences.t:
et calido velamina tincta cruore
dat munus raptae velut inritamen amoris.
sentences.l: and the coverings steeped in the warm gore he gives as a gift to the woman he had seized, as if a goad of love.
sentences.i: and he gives the garment soaked in the warm gore to the woman he had carried off, a present, as though it were a charm to rouse love.
sentences.n: “raptae” is the poem’s own participle for Deianira, “to her who had been seized”: Ovid does not soften what Nessus attempted, and the gift goes to that same woman. “munus” is a predicative accusative, “gives it as a gift”, and “velut” marks the pretence in “inritamen amoris”, “a goad of love” — the word for a spur, and a lie.

sentences.t:
Longa fuit medii mora temporis, actaque magni
Herculis inplerant terras odiumque novercae.
sentences.l: Long was the delay of the time in between, and the deeds of great Hercules had filled the lands and his stepmother’s hatred.
sentences.i: A long stretch of time went by between, and the deeds of great Hercules had filled the world — and filled his stepmother’s hatred.
sentences.n: “inplerant” is the syncopated pluperfect for “impleverant”, and it works as a zeugma: it governs “terras” literally, “filled the lands”, and “odium novercae” figuratively, “filled up the stepmother’s hatred”. The stepmother is Juno, whose grudge against Jupiter’s son is fed by every labour he finishes.

sentences.t:
Victor ab Oechalia Cenaeo sacra parabat
vota Iovi, cum Fama loquax praecessit ad aures,
Deianira, tuas,
sentences.l: Victorious from Oechalia, he was preparing the sacred rites vowed to Cenaean Jove, when talkative Rumour ran on ahead to your ears, Deianira,
sentences.i: Home in victory from Oechalia, he was setting out the offerings he had vowed to Jove of Cenaeum, when chattering Rumour got first to your ears, Deianira —
sentences.n: “sacra … vota” is one phrase, the rites he had vowed, and “Cenaeo … Iovi” is Jupiter as worshipped at Cenaeum, the headland of Euboea. This is the inverted “cum”, where the main clause sets the scene and the “cum” clause brings the event; and Ovid breaks off into apostrophe, speaking to Deianira as “tuas”, exactly as he spoke to Nessus at line 101.

sentences.t:
quae veris addere falsa
gaudet et e minimo sua per mendacia crescit,
Amphitryoniaden Ioles ardore teneri.
sentences.l: she who delights to add false things to true and grows out of the least through her own lies — that the son of Amphitryon was held by passion for Iole.
sentences.i: Rumour, who loves to add the false to the true and swells from the least beginning by her own lying — the report being that Amphitryon’s son was in the grip of a passion for Iole.
sentences.n: “veris” and “falsa” are neuter plural adjectives used as nouns, “true things” and “false things”, in the dative and accusative after “addere”. The infinitive clause “Amphitryoniaden … teneri” is the content of the rumour, hanging on “Fama praecessit”; “Amphitryoniaden” is a Greek accusative of the patronymic and “Ioles” a Greek genitive.

sentences.l: The woman in love believes it, and, terrified by the report of a new love, gave way at first to tears, and by weeping poured out her grief, pitiable;
sentences.i: Loving him, she believes it; terrified by the report of a new love, she gave way to tears at first, and, poor woman, wept her grief out;
sentences.n: “credit” is a present among perfects, the narrative quickening for the instant that decides everything, and “amans” is a feminine participle used as a noun: her love is why she believes. “flendo” is an ablative gerund, “by weeping”, and “miseranda”, a gerundive used as an adjective, “fit to be pitied”, is the poet’s judgement breaking into her sentence.

sentences.t:
mox deinde “quid autem
flemus?” ait “paelex lacrimis laetabitur istis.
sentences.l: then presently she says, “But why do we weep? The mistress will rejoice at these tears.
sentences.i: then, soon after: “But why are we weeping? My husband’s mistress will be glad of tears like these.
sentences.n: “paelex” is a hard word — the woman who takes a place beside the wife — and it is Deianira’s word for Iole, not the poem’s: Iole comes out of the sack of Oechalia and has no say in any of it. “laetabitur” is a deponent future taking the ablative “lacrimis … istis”, and “istis” keeps the dismissive edge that “iste” carries, “tears like these”. “flemus”, “we weep”, is the same poetic plural for “I” that Hercules used at line 122.

sentences.t:
Quae quoniam adveniet, properandum aliquidque novandum est,
dum licet et nondum thalamos tenet altera nostros.
sentences.l: And since she will arrive, there must be hurrying and something must be made new, while it is still allowed and while another woman does not yet hold my marriage chamber.
sentences.i: And since she is coming, I must hurry and try something new, while I still may, and while no other woman holds my bed.
sentences.n: “Quae” is a connecting relative opening the sentence, “and since she …”. “properandum … novandum est” is the impersonal gerundive of obligation with no agent expressed — the Latin says only that hurrying must be done, which is bleaker than “I must hurry” — and “thalamos … nostros” is a poetic plural for her one marriage bed.

sentences.t:
Conquerar an sileam? Repetam Calydona morerne?
Excedam tectis an, si nihil amplius, obstem?
sentences.l: Shall I complain, or keep silent? Shall I go back to Calydon, or die? Shall I leave the house, or — if nothing more — stand in the way?
sentences.i: Am I to complain or say nothing? To go back to Calydon, or to die? To walk out of the house, or, if nothing else, to block her path?
sentences.n: Six deliberative subjunctives in two lines, the mood of a mind that cannot settle: “conquerar” and “morer” are deponent, “sileam, repetam, excedam, obstem” active. “morerne” is “morer” with the enclitic “-ne” doing the work of “an”; “Calydona” is a Greek accusative, her father’s city; “tectis” is an ablative of separation.

sentences.t:
Quid si me, Meleagre, tuam memor esse sororem
forte paro facinus, quantumque iniuria possit
femineusque dolor, iugulata paelice testor?”
sentences.l: What if I, Meleager, remembering that I am your sister, perhaps make ready a crime, and, with the mistress’s throat cut, bear witness how much an injury and a woman’s grief can do?”
sentences.i: What if I, Meleager, remembering whose sister I am, set some crime in motion, and with that mistress’s throat cut show what a wrong and a woman’s grief can do?”
sentences.n: She breaks off to address her dead brother Meleager — an apostrophe inside a speech, and an appeal to the family she comes from rather than the one she married into. “memor” takes the accusative and infinitive “me … esse sororem”; “quantum … possit” is an indirect question after “testor”; and “iugulata paelice” is a genuine ablative absolute, “with the mistress’s throat cut”, the murder imagined as already done.

sentences.t:
In cursus animus varios abit: omnibus illis
praetulit inbutam Nesseo sanguine vestem
mittere, quae vires defecto reddat amori.
sentences.l: Her mind goes off into various courses: to all of those she preferred to send the robe steeped in Nessus’s blood, which might give back its strength to a love that had failed.
sentences.i: Her mind runs off down one course after another; to all of them she preferred sending the robe soaked in Nessus’s blood, to give a failing love its strength back.
sentences.n: “praefero” takes a dative of what is passed over, “omnibus illis”, and here has an infinitive, “mittere”, as the thing preferred. “quae … reddat” is a relative clause of purpose, hence the subjunctive — the robe is sent in order to restore — and “defecto … amori” is the dative with “reddat”, a love that has given out.

sentences.t:
Ignaroque Lichae, quid tradat, nescia, luctus
ipsa suos tradit blandisque (miserrima!) verbis,
dona det illa viro, mandat.
sentences.l: And to Lichas, who did not know, herself not knowing what she was handing over, she hands over her own griefs, and with coaxing words — most wretched woman! — she charges him to give those gifts to her husband.
sentences.i: And to Lichas, who knew nothing — she herself knowing nothing of what she handed him — she handed over her own sorrows, and with coaxing words (poor wretch) told him to give the gift to her husband.
sentences.n: Two ignorances stand side by side, “ignaro … Lichae” in the dative and “nescia” of Deianira in the nominative, with the indirect question “quid tradat” between them. “luctus … suos tradit” is the cruelty of the sentence — what she hands over is, in the event, her own mourning — while “dona det illa viro” is a bare subjunctive after “mandat”, with no “ut”, and the parenthesis “miserrima!” is the poet breaking in.

sentences.t:
Capit inscius heros
induiturque umeris Lernaeae virus echidnae.
sentences.l: The hero takes it, not knowing, and puts on over his shoulders the venom of the Lernaean viper.
sentences.i: The hero takes it, knowing nothing, and draws over his shoulders the venom of the Lernaean snake.
sentences.n: “induitur” is a middle use of the passive — he clothes himself — which is why it still keeps an accusative object, “virus”, with “umeris” the dative of the part clothed. Ovid names not the robe but what is in it: the poison has come snake to arrow, arrow to centaur, centaur to shirt, and only the last step is invisible to the man putting it on.

sentences.t:
Tura dabat primis et verba precantia flammis
vinaque marmoreas patera fundebat in aras:
sentences.l: He was giving incense and praying words to the first flames, and was pouring wine from a bowl onto the marble altars:
sentences.i: He was giving the first flames their incense and his words of prayer, and pouring wine from the bowl over the marble altars —
sentences.n: One verb, “dabat”, serves two objects of quite different kinds, incense and prayers: a syllepsis, and the kind of yoking Ovid likes. The imperfects hold the ritual in progress until a perfect breaks it in the next line, and “patera” is the flat bowl used for libation, an ablative of means.

sentences.t:
incaluit vis illa mali resolutaque flammis
Herculeos abiit late dilapsa per artus.
sentences.l: that force of the evil grew warm, and, loosened by the flames, went off, spreading widely, through Hercules’ limbs.
sentences.i: the force of the poison grew warm, and, melted by the flames, went its way, spreading wide through the limbs of Hercules.
sentences.n: “vis illa mali” is deliberately vague, “that power of the bad thing”, because nobody in the scene knows what it is. The heat of his own sacrifice is what wakes it: two participles hang on the one verb, “resoluta” for the melting and “dilapsa” for the running everywhere afterwards.

sentences.l: While he could, he pressed the groan back with his accustomed courage; after his endurance was conquered by the agonies, he shoved the altars away and filled wooded Oeta with his cries.
sentences.i: As long as he could, he forced the groan back with the courage that was his habit; once his endurance was beaten by the pain, he thrust the altars aside and filled the woods of Oeta with his shouting.
sentences.n: “solita … virtute” is an ablative of means split around its own object, “gemitum”: the courage is his by habit, and it is the first thing the poison takes. “postquam” stands inside its own clause, which is split around it — “victa malis … est patientia” — and “Oeten” is a Greek accusative, the wooded mountain that the shouting fills.

sentences.t:
Nec mora, letiferam conatur scindere vestem:
qua trahitur, trahit illa cutem,
sentences.l: No delay — he tries to tear the death-bringing robe: where it is dragged, it drags the skin,
sentences.i: There is no pause: he tries to rip the death-carrying robe off; wherever it is pulled, it pulls the skin with it,
sentences.n: “Nec mora” is a bare noun doing the work of a whole clause, “and there was no delay”. The line turns on one verb used twice, passive and then active, “qua trahitur, trahit”, so that the pulling comes straight back on him; “qua” is “where, at whatever point”.

sentences.t:
foedumque relatu,
aut haeret membris frustra temptata revelli,
aut laceros artus et grandia detegit ossa.
sentences.l: and — foul in the telling — either it sticks to the limbs, tried in vain to be torn away, or it lays bare mangled limbs and huge bones.
sentences.i: and — it is foul to tell — either it holds fast to the flesh, pulled at in vain, or it strips bare the torn limbs and the great bones.
sentences.n: “relatu” is a supine in “-u”, the form that follows adjectives like “foedum”, “foul with respect to the telling”, and the neuter “foedum” stands in apposition to the whole clause. “temptata revelli” puts a passive infinitive after a passive participle, a Greek turn of phrase; “grandia … ossa” is scale, not decoration — the bones laid bare are outsize, as the body is.

sentences.t:
Ipse cruor, gelido ceu quondam lamina candens
tincta lacu, stridit coquiturque ardente veneno.
sentences.l: The gore itself hisses, as a white-hot blade sometimes does when dipped in a cold pool, and is boiled by the burning poison.
sentences.i: The gore itself hisses — as a white-hot blade will when it is plunged into cold water — and is boiled by the burning venom.
sentences.n: “ceu” introduces the simile, and “quondam” inside one means “as sometimes happens”, not “once upon a time”: the picture is a smith quenching iron, the glowing blade hissing as it goes under. “coquitur”, “is boiled”, keeps the forge in the sentence to the end — but the heat has changed sides, since here it is the liquid that is brought to the boil.
